children: By Lizzy Lawrence
When Belen Garijo took the helm of French drug giant Sanofi earlier this year, she was met with deep skepticism from Wall Street.

The 66-year-old pharmaceutical executive came from running a German drugmaker half the size of Sanofi. Investors didn't think she had the chops to shake up Sanofi, which has struggled to find the next generation of blockbusters to power sales.
News of her appointment sent Sanofi's stock down nearly 5%.

On Tuesday, Garijo showed she isn't afraid of making substantive changes when she reached the biggest pharmaceutical transaction of the year, a $41 billion deal to buy biotech Insmed. Shares surged nearly 10%.
"It is a critical step forward in our strategy that is already in motion," she said after the deal was announced.

The move puts Garijo's stamp on an urgent corporate reclamation effort. With the deal, the new CEO is betting she can fill an almost $20 billion void when its top-selling drug Dupixent goes off patent in coming years.
But it puts a lot of money at stake, leaving Sanofi with less room to pivot if Insmed drug sales don't perform as expected. The company said it is taking on some debt to do the deal.

"It's impressive to see Belen step up to execute such a substantial transaction," said Leerink analyst David Risinger. "It is larger than many in the investment community anticipated, but it fits extremely well."

Garijo, a physician from Spain, worked at Sanofi earlier in her career and helped integrate the biotech Genzyme. She joined Germany's Merck KGaA in 2011, where she rose through the ranks to become CEO and chair of the executive board.
In some of her first comments to Sanofi's shareholders, she promised to set "clear priorities and an ambitious road map" for the drugmaker.
Garijo also came out early talking about the potential for Sanofi to do big takeovers.

"Traditionally, Sanofi has been on smaller deals, bolt-ons to eventually increase innovation or fill gaps," she said on her first earnings call over the summer. "I think our appetite for bigger deals is an option."

Sanofi decided to move forward with the Insmed deal not long after Garijo started in May. Insmed is a rare disease drugmaker with two approved respiratory drugs and several different medications under development. The company expects sales from Insmed's drugs to exceed $10 billion over the next decade.
"We are acquiring an established business with significant growth potential, and not simply investing in future scientific promise," Garijo said.
Sanofi executives defended the size of the deal on the investor call, saying the company still has room to pursue other small acquisitions.

The acquisition of Insmed bolsters Sanofi's respiratory franchise, which brought in around 40% of sales last year. Insmed brings two approved drugs for rare respiratory diseases that notched $600 million in sales last year along with experimental treatments for several lung diseases and neuromuscular diseases such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

Jefferies analysts said in a note that they liked the price of the deal and noted it brings two already-successful drugs to Sanofi that can also be expanded to other diseases. While it doesn't single-handedly solve Sanofi's struggle to find innovative drugs, they said, "it buys time."
Still, this may not be a done deal.
"Although topping bids post deal announcements are extremely uncommon in biotech M&A, we cannot rule out another company bidding a higher price," Risinger said.
